description: A very tight project schedule and time pressure forced the usability consultants to work at high speed with only two consultants, compressing user research and design activities.
justification: Limited time reduced designers' capacity to run iterative cycles, thoroughly involve stakeholders, and perform slower, deeper synthesis and evaluation (integrate feedback & iteration; facilitate user involvement; evaluate designs).
reference_excerpt: The project group had worked for five months nailing down the organizational requirements and their time was running out. ... Therefore the UCD process could not take more than eight weeks. ... it was judged that we would be able to deliver on time by working with two consultants on top speed.

source_text_file: E and H - 2004 - Procuring a usable system using unemployed personas.txt
description: Members of the procurement project group (PPG) only participated occasionally in hands-on research and only one member was allowed to attend each interview, limiting direct stakeholder involvement.
justification: Restricted stakeholder presence hindered designers' ability to facilitate user involvement, build shared understanding, and coordinate decisions with the procurers (facilitate user involvement; coordinate multidisciplinary team; manage user understanding).
reference_excerpt: Although they were active and engaged, the members of the PPG, on the other hand, only participated occasionally in the hands-on work, such as on an interview or in a design session and then got the results presented to them in a weekly workshop. In order to not interfere too much with the actual interviews only one member of the PPG was allowed to attend on each interview session.

description: Organizational requirements were abstract, diffuse or contradictory and had not been detailed to the same level as user requirements.
justification: This lack of concrete organizational specification prevented designers and procurers from aligning business goals with design decisions and impeded iterative decision-making and integration of user and organizational requirements (manage user understanding; integrate feedback & iteration; specify user requirements).
reference_excerpt: We identified the organizational requirements first and they did not reach the same level of concretization as the users’ requirements. ... Of course, there were still questions that were unanswered and even some contradictions in the documents on organizational requirements, but we expected these to be resolved during the second iteration.

description: A perceived power imbalance occurred where the usability company was seen as 'too strong' and more professional, leaving the PPG feeling unable to steer or own design decisions.
justification: This emotional and trust-related tension reduced the PPG's confidence and willingness to accept or champion design outcomes, forcing designers to pause work to rebuild shared understanding (facilitate user involvement; coordinate multidisciplinary team; integrate feedback & iteration).
reference_excerpt: but then… the usability company got to strong somehow. The usability company was much more professional in some way – they had their methodology and they knew where to go and so forth. But we, who sat with the organizational requirements, in which the usability company did not have any competence, we were not as good at steering, so to speak.

justification: Reduced user evaluation limited designers' ability to study context of use and validate information architecture choices, weakening the evidence base for design decisions (evaluate designs; understand context of use).
reference_excerpt: Card-sorting exercises were planned with the two most important user groups, but only one could be performed.

justification: Limited design literacy among stakeholders increased the effort designers needed to coordinate the team and communicate decisions, hindering shared decision-making and smooth iteration (coordinate multidisciplinary team; manage user understanding; facilitate user involvement).
reference_excerpt: Since the members had varying experiences of working with design the discussion was not always smooth and concepts such as navigation levels had got to be explained.

justification: Remote/outsourced working arrangements limited stakeholder immersion and on-site collaboration, making it harder to facilitate involvement and build organizational ownership (facilitate user involvement; coordinate multidisciplinary team).
reference_excerpt: they comment that they should have participated more in the activities and that all work should have been done in their offices, instead of having the usability consultants work in their own office.

source_text_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.txt
description: Intercontinental location differences combined with the COVID-19 pandemic limited availability and direct communication with target users in rural Africa, constraining engagement.
justification: This reduced the team's ability to facilitate user involvement and to maintain deep, evolving user understanding (and limited opportunities to study real contexts of use), impeding participatory evaluation and contextual inquiry.
reference_excerpt: The particular challenge in this project is the intercontinental and intercultural communication with the user groups on-site since the development team consists of German physicians and computer scientists. The user groups are primarily located in rural areas of Africa, especially Madagascar. Another constraint is the currently active COVID-19 pandemic, which leads to severe limitations in the availability and communication ability of the relevant user groups, especially in Africa.

source_json_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.json
source_text_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.txt
description: The team lacked sufficient shared language skills with users, requiring interpreters for interviews and evaluations.
justification: Relying on interpreters constrained direct communication and nuance, hindering designers' ability to manage user understanding, elicit deep insights, and run smooth participatory evaluations.
reference_excerpt: The participatory evaluations take place via intercontinental video conferences. The video conferences happen either in French or Malagasy, depending on the user group. Due to the lack of language skills, interpreters are present in addition to the direct participants of the evaluation.

source_json_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.json
source_text_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.txt
description: Socio-cultural hierarchies and gender dynamics caused some participants not to speak freely in certain interview or evaluation settings.
justification: This trust and cultural participation issue limited facilitators' ability to involve users honestly and fully, reducing the quality of user insights needed to inform requirements and scenarios.
reference_excerpt: we first had to learn, with the help of resident physicians, that certain interview settings did not produce the needed outcome because, due to socio-cultural differences, certain groups of people did not express themselves freely or at all in some settings, which is a major problem for participatory design methods.

source_text_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.txt
description: Limited and unstable local IT infrastructure in primary health care facilities reduced users' ability to use online tools and participate remotely.
justification: Poor connectivity and partial infrastructure hindered participatory evaluation (e.g., sharing prototypes, uploading images) and limited designers' ability to observe real usage workflows and test prototypes in realistic conditions.
reference_excerpt: The results of the interviews allowed us to obtain a detailed picture of the participant’s level of knowledge about FGS and the working conditions existing in rural areas of Africa, particularly Madagascar. In general, there was little experience with FGS. Stable IT infrastructure was only partially present in primary health care facilities.

source_text_file: Lehmann et al. - 2022 - Designing AINA Intercultural Human Centered Design of an AI based Application for Supporting the Dia.txt
description: The team could not perform desired on-site observations during analysis and evaluation because of the global COVID-19 pandemic.
justification: The inability to conduct in-person contextual inquiry prevented designers from fully understanding the context of use and limited the depth of ethnographic data that would inform requirements and iterations.
reference_excerpt: Since user behavior plays a crucial role in any technology, we wished to conduct additional on-site observations during the analysis and evaluation phases. Unfortunately, this was not possible due to the global COVID-19 pandemic.

description: Regulatory and guideline constraints (AI/medical device guidance) prevented simplification of technical language in the manual.
justification: External regulatory requirements limited the team's ability to adapt documentation language to users, hindering management of user understanding and the holistic user experience despite iterative feedback.
reference_excerpt: Unfortunately, the revision of the manual, based on AI guidelines for medical devices, did not reduce the number of technical terms used, so all users commented negatively on this.

source_text_file: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt
description: The team used a semi-structured design process without a strict schedule, which sped production but reduced experimental rigor and produced heterogeneous testing stimuli.
justification: This process-level constraint limited the designers' ability to perform rigorous evaluation and to integrate feedback consistently across iterations, hindering evaluate designs and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: In the current study, we chose to implement a semi-structured design process that refrained from using a strict schedule to determine when to begin testing and making interface improvements during the design of the interface. This methodology increased the speed at which the interface could be produced at the cost of rigorous experimental design.

source_text_file: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt
description: The user testing had a low sample size, limiting the statistical and generalizable strength of evaluation findings.
justification: A small participant pool constrained the designers' ability to evaluate designs comprehensively and to draw reliable conclusions needed for subsequent iteration and specification of requirements.
reference_excerpt: Aside from a low sample size, the main limitation of the user testing portion of our evaluation is the lack of a homologous "stimuli" to test with participants.

source_text_file: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt
description: Participant sample was unrepresentative: 71% had prior health-care work experience and all reported some familiarity with the tests shown.
justification: This interactional bias limited designers' ability to manage authentic user understanding and to facilitate involvement of typical (naïve) patients, reducing the validity of insights used to specify user requirements and evaluate designs.
reference_excerpt: An additional limitation that may affect the generalizability of the results of this study is the large percentage (71 percent) of patients who had history of working in health care prior to participating in this study. ... All participants indicated they had some familiarity with the tests presented in the test result interface.

source_text_file: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt
description: Each participant was allowed to use only one version of the interface and could not participate in later sessions.
justification: This recruitment/design choice prevented designers from tracking how individual users responded across iterations, making it harder to integrate feedback longitudinally and to evaluate the effects of changes across versions.
reference_excerpt: To avoid skewing the perceptions and results of the later versions of the test result interface, participants were only invited to use one version of the interface and were not allowed to participate again after their initial testing session.

source_text_file: Nystrom DT - 2018 - Methods for Patient Centered Interface Design of Test Result Display in Online Portals.txt
description: Design changes produced non-linear visual scales, but the team did not assess the impact of these non-linear scales on patient perceptions.
justification: Failing to evaluate this design consequence limited the designers' ability to understand contextual effects and holistic experience, constraining the evaluate designs and integrate feedback & iteration workloads.
reference_excerpt: An unanticipated consequence of this design adjustment was the creation of non-linear scales, where the visual space for each biomarker are radically different than the other. We did not make any attempt to assess the impact of these non-linear scales on patient perceptions.

description: The interface used a red/green color scheme but the study did not include confirmed colorblind participants to evaluate accessibility.
justification: This oversight limited designers' ability to evaluate and address accessibility in the real context of use, hindering the evaluate designs and address holistic experience workloads.
reference_excerpt: An additional limitation ... the use of red/green color schemes for the design of our interface could potentially limit the ease of using this interface for colorblind patients. While to our knowledge none of the test subjects were red/green color blind, we should note that "color" was not the only indicator that subjects had available to help them understand the meaning of the graphs or displays.

justification: Remote-only data collection constrained the team's ability to understand real-world contexts of use and to evaluate designs under typical conditions, hindering the workloads of understanding context of use and evaluating designs.

description: Usability testing relied on a desktop mobile-device emulator rather than testing on actual smartphones, reducing fidelity of interaction data.
justification: Using an emulator limited the team's ability to detect usability problems specific to real mobile use, impeding evaluation of designs and understanding context of use needed for iteration.
reference_excerpt: We used only an emulator on a desktop computer to test our medium-fidelity mHealth prototype; thus, it is possible that some usability problems were not detected. In the future, the prototype should be tested on a smartphone to approximate real use conditions.

description: Convenience sampling recruited participants with prior exposure to bone-health studies or clinic care, biasing the participant pool toward more informed users.
justification: This recruitment bias limited the designers' ability to manage a representative, evolving understanding of diverse users and to facilitate involvement of less informed users, affecting the workloads of managing user understanding and facilitating user involvement.
reference_excerpt: Second, convenience sampling may have biased our results, as we recruited participants who had participated in previous studies on bone health or who had been evaluated in orthopedic clinics at our center. Design workshop participants were well aware of osteoporosis and its negative impacts and may have had prior knowledge related to injury management.

description: The usability protocol required participants to have Zoom and a computer, which selected for participants with higher technological literacy.
justification: This inclusion requirement constrained participation of low-tech users and hindered designers' ability to understand and evaluate the app for less tech-literate segments, affecting understanding context of use and facilitating user involvement.
reference_excerpt: Third, the protocol for the usability tests required participants to have access to Zoom. Consequently, these participants likely had higher technological literacy than those who would never have used videoconferencing tools.

description: Some participants skipped tutorial pop-ups because they were too long or insufficiently motivating, reducing engagement with onboarding content.
justification: Participant disengagement with tutorials impeded designers' ability to ensure users learned key interactions and to evaluate comprehension, limiting efforts to integrate feedback and evaluate designs accurately.
reference_excerpt: As the participants navigated to access different functionalities of our app, tutorials appeared as pop-ups on how to use the functionality. A few participants skipped some of the tutorials and noted that they were too long.

description: High cognitive load and poorly phrased questions caused participants to omit or enter incorrect information, and many struggled to recall medication names and dosages during testing.
justification: These user cognitive limitations and question formulation issues limited the designers' ability to evaluate data-entry interactions and to specify robust user requirements for input fields and workflows.
reference_excerpt: In addition, most participants had trouble remembering which medications and dosages they were prescribed when the app asked them to input their prescriptions. Some questions in the app were poorly formulated; for example, participants expressed confusion over a question in the profile setup, which asked, “Were you prescribed or recommended to take acetaminophen for your pain?”

description: Frequent iterative changes across prototypes (including adding content in one iteration and deleting it in the next) created additional coordination and workload for the research team.
justification: This complexity hindered the team's ability to efficiently integrate feedback & iteration and to coordinate multidisciplinary team activities needed to maintain coherent design direction.
reference_excerpt: There were instances where new content added during a previous iteration, was deleted for the subsequent iteration based on user-feedback. Although those details are outside of the scope of this paper, we plan to report them with results of the quantitative pilot test.

description: Design work was constrained by existing infrastructure and templates, requiring trade-offs between fidelity to user data, existing resources, university website templates, and visual design.
justification: These infrastructural constraints limited the team's ability to produce design solutions and to fully address the holistic experience and information architecture they wanted to implement.
reference_excerpt: The prototype design process involved using an interdisciplinary and user-centered lens to balance fidelity to the data, the use of existing resources, infrastructure (ie, a university website template) and visual design.

description: Unclear ethical, privacy, and scope boundaries for the planned 'Ask ALEX' feedback mechanism created uncertainty about how to offer interactive, individualized feedback.
justification: This uncertainty impeded the team's ability to facilitate user involvement and to implement an interactive feedback loop safely, affecting evaluation and ongoing iteration of that feature.
reference_excerpt: While a feedback mechanism of this kind may present barriers that still need to be addressed as the prototype progresses (eg, making it clear that the team cannot provide medical advice, being explicit about the level of privacy, deciding if connecting participants to local resources is within the scope of the project), user requests made it clear that individualizing the information processing experience was of interest.

description: Technical and resourcing limitations left the VHA prototype without accessibility and media features (no subtitles and no animations) that the team planned to add later.
justification: Lack of these features constrained the designers' ability to address holistic user experience and evaluate accessibility and synchronized multimedia presentations during prototyping.
reference_excerpt: Did not have subtitles in the VHA prototype however, based on previous work in this area and in accordance with ADA guidelines, we plan to build and test a final version with subtitles to enhance accessibility. The current VHA does not include added animations. Plans to include animations in updated prototypes will follow best practices related to synchronizing

source_text_file: Vilaro et al. - 2023 - Information Architects Using Community Engaged and Qualitative Methods to Design a Technology Based.txt
description: The brief VHA interaction and a single infographic could not accommodate the breadth of user-requested supplemental information, forcing the team to design and maintain a separate website.
justification: This limitation required additional production of design solutions (a supplemental website) and increased workload to manage aligned content and avoid cognitive overload while preserving the VHA's brevity.
reference_excerpt: As data was reviewed, it became clear that a single infographic may not be able to accommodate the breadth of additional information that was being requested. Second, because participants agreed that the brief VHA interaction itself was “just right” in terms of length and information density, any additional information would need to be provided outside of the VHA content. Third, many participants suggested a website while viewing the infographic, citing their view that because different people might want to know about different information, an infographic would be too busy and dense if it were to accommodate the diversity of user needs.
